prompt: Write a short fable about a lemur and a light bulb.
generations:
Every evening, a lemur watched a light bulb shine through the window of a forest hut.

“What a splendid creature,” he said. “It glows without gathering firewood or chasing fireflies.”

Determined to learn its secret, he slipped inside and asked, “How do you make so much light?”

“I don’t do it alone,” said the bulb. “A wire brings me power.”

But the lemur scarcely listened. He unscrewed the bulb and carried it home, certain its brilliance would make him admired throughout the forest.

In his tree, the bulb stayed dark.

“You’ve lost your gift!” the lemur cried.

“No,” said the bulb. “You’ve mistaken me for everything that helped me shine.”

The lemur returned it to the hut. After that, when he admired a bright light, he remembered the unseen wire.

**Moral: No one shines entirely alone.**

Each night, a lemur watched a light bulb glow through the window of a forest cottage.

“What a splendid creature,” he said. “It shines without gathering a single firefly.”

Determined to impress it, he leaped among the branches, showing off his finest tricks. The bulb offered no applause.

“You think you’re better than me?” the lemur demanded.

Just then, the cottage owner switched off the light.

The lemur waited for it to return. But the moon rose, the crickets sang, and still the bulb stayed dark.

At last, he climbed home, finding his way by the stars.

**Moral: Admire another’s gifts, but don’t forget your own.**

A lemur found a light bulb on the forest floor and hung it above his branch.

“Now I shall have light all night,” he told the fireflies. “You may go.”

But when darkness came, the bulb stayed dark. The lemur shook it, polished it, and sternly reminded it of its purpose.

At last, a firefly returned.

“Why won’t it shine?” the lemur asked.

“It needs power,” said the firefly.

The lemur looked from the splendid glass bulb to the tiny glow hovering beside him.

“Would you and your friends stay?” he asked.

“We would,” said the firefly, “if you’d ask instead of dismiss.”

**Moral: Value the help you have, not merely the promise of something brighter.**

A lemur found a light bulb glowing in a ranger’s window.

“What a clever little sun,” he said. “Teach me to shine, and I’ll never need anyone to guide me through the forest.”

“I cannot shine by myself,” said the bulb. “A wire brings me power.”

The lemur scoffed. “Then you’re not so clever after all.”

That night, he set off alone beneath the dark trees. When he lost his way, a firefly offered to lead him home.

“I need no help,” the lemur began. Then he remembered the bulb—and followed the tiny light.

**Moral: Accepting help does not make your own light less bright.**

Every evening, a lemur climbed to the village lantern and admired the light bulb inside.

“How generous I am,” said the bulb, “to give everyone light.”

“You do shine beautifully,” said the lemur.

One night, the bulb went dark.

“Fetch me a new filament!” it demanded. “Polish my glass!”

Instead, the lemur followed a wire down the tree and found a loose plug. He pushed it into its socket, and the bulb glowed again.

For a while, the bulb said nothing.

Then it called down, “Thank you.”

The lemur smiled. “You might thank the wire, too.”

**Moral: Even those who shine depend on others.**

Every evening, a lemur named Luma sat beneath a bare light bulb and boasted, “See how the moths gather? They admire my beautiful tail.”

The bulb said nothing. It simply shone.

One night, a storm knocked out the power. The moths scattered, and Luma found herself alone in the dark.

“Where are my admirers?” she cried.

“They were never yours,” said the bulb.

Ashamed, Luma climbed down. When the power returned, she noticed that the bulb’s light also showed beetles a safe path across the floor.

“Can I help?” she asked.

“Move your tail,” said the bulb. “You’re blocking the way.”

And she did.

**Moral:** It is better to help others shine than to mistake their light for your own.

Every night, a lemur sat beneath a light bulb outside the village shop and boasted, “See how brightly my tree shines!”

“You did not make the light,” said a moth.

“But I discovered the branch closest to it,” replied the lemur, fluffing his tail.

One evening, the bulb burned out. The lemur shook the branch, scolded the darkness, and demanded that the moth admire him anyway.

Instead, the moth fetched the shopkeeper, who fitted a new bulb.

When the light returned, the lemur was unusually quiet.

“Well?” asked the moth.

The lemur climbed down and thanked the shopkeeper.

**Moral: Enjoy the light, but remember who keeps it burning.**

A lemur found a light bulb beneath a tree and held it up to the sun.

“Look!” he told the other animals. “I have caught the daylight. Tonight, my branch will shine.”

But when darkness fell, the bulb stayed dark.

“Perhaps it needs encouragement,” said the lemur. He praised it, polished it, and shook it gently. Nothing happened.

An old tortoise passing below looked up. “That bulb needs electricity, not applause.”

The lemur’s ears drooped. “Then I’ve made a foolish boast.”

“Yes,” said the tortoise. “But you needn’t make another.”

The next morning, the lemur asked how light bulbs worked.

**Moral: Looking bright is not the same as understanding.**

A lemur found a glowing light bulb hanging outside a village hut.

“What a marvelous fruit!” he cried. “Even the moon would envy its shine.”

“It isn’t fruit,” said a moth.

“You’re only saying that because you want it,” replied the lemur.

He climbed the wall and reached for the bulb, but its heat sent him tumbling into a basket of laundry.

The moth settled on the basket’s rim. “Still hungry?”

“Yes,” grumbled the lemur, rubbing his paw. “But I think I’ll look for something less impressive.”

**Moral: What dazzles the eye may not nourish the belly.**

A lemur found a light bulb beneath a traveler’s abandoned tent.

“What a splendid fruit!” he cried. “It must hold the sweetest juice in the forest.”

He bit it gently, then shook it, but the bulb offered nothing.

An old tortoise passing by said, “Not everything round is meant to be eaten.”

“Then it’s useless,” said the lemur.

That evening, the traveler returned. She fitted the bulb into her lantern and switched it on. Warm light spilled across the clearing, revealing the lemur’s lost little brother crouched beside a stump.

The lemur hurried to him, then looked back at the glowing bulb.

“No juice,” he admitted, “but something worth having.”

**Moral: Before calling something useless, learn what it is for.**

prompt: Write a short story that has three main characters Alice Bob and Mallory.
generations:
Alice found the key inside a loaf of bread.

She had baked the loaf herself, which made this particularly annoying.

“Perhaps you put it in with the flour,” Bob suggested. He owned the bakery next door and had come over to borrow cinnamon, as he did every Tuesday.

“I think I would remember owning a silver key with teeth shaped like birds.”

From the window seat, Mallory lowered her newspaper.

“Depends how tired you were.”

Alice brushed crumbs from the key. A paper tag hung from its handle.

**WEST STATION. LOCKER 13. BEFORE NOON.**

The clock above the oven read eleven forty-two.

“We should go,” Bob said.

“We should finish breakfast,” said Mallory.

Alice was already taking off her apron.

West Station had been abandoned for twenty years. Weeds grew between the tracks, and the station clock had lost both hands. Inside, beneath a peeling departure board, stood a row of lockers.

There was no number thirteen.

“Twelve, fourteen, fifteen,” Bob counted.

Mallory folded her arms. “A wasted journey. How surprising.”

Alice crouched beside locker fourteen. Beneath its brass plate, two screw holes marked where another number had once been fixed.

She inserted the key.

Inside lay a small wooden box and a photograph of three children standing beside the station fountain.

Alice recognized herself immediately: missing front tooth, furious expression. Bob stood beside her holding a frog.

The third child wore Mallory’s red scarf.

“We knew each other?” Bob whispered.

Mallory said nothing.

Alice opened the box.

Inside were three glass marbles, a train ticket punched with a star, and a folded promise:

**We will come back when we are grown. We will remember where the train goes. We will not let Mallory go alone.**

A whistle sounded beyond the platform.

Bob dropped the photograph.

Through the dusty windows, a train was arriving on tracks that moments ago had been covered in weeds. Its carriages glowed green, and rain streamed down its windows, though the sky outside was clear.

Mallory took the ticket from the box.

“I wasn’t going to ask,” she said.

Alice looked at her friend—at the packed bag tucked beneath her coat, the way her fingers trembled.

“You put the key in my bread.”

“I wasn’t going to ask directly.”

Beyond the window, a conductor opened a carriage door.

“Is it dangerous?” Bob asked.

“Yes,” Mallory said.

“Will there be breakfast?”

“I don’t remember.”

Bob sighed and pulled a paper bag from his pocket. “Good thing I brought these.”

Alice locked the empty locker. She almost left the key in the door, then thought better of it.

Together they crossed the platform. Mallory climbed aboard first, and this time, when she turned to look behind her, the other two were there.

Alice found the door at the bottom of the library’s return bin.

“Doors don’t belong there,” Bob said.

“Neither did the sandwich you returned last Tuesday.”

“That was a bookmark.”

Mallory leaned over the counter. The door was no bigger than a dictionary, painted blue, with a brass handle that turned beneath her fingertip.

Beyond it stretched a moonlit railway platform.

A whistle sounded.

“We should tell someone,” Bob said.

Alice had already climbed through. Mallory followed, and Bob, who disliked adventures but disliked being left out more, squeezed after them.

On the platform stood a train with three carriages. Its destination board read:

**THINGS YOU MEANT TO SAY**

“Oh,” Mallory said quietly.

Alice stopped reaching for the nearest carriage door.

Bob looked back. The little blue door had vanished.

A ticket machine clattered. Three slips of paper dropped into its tray.

Alice’s read: **I’M SORRY.**

Bob’s read: **PLEASE STAY.**

Mallory’s read: **IT WAS ME.**

For a moment, none of them spoke.

Then Alice turned to Mallory. “I’m sorry I told everyone you were moving before you’d decided.”

Mallory folded her ticket in half.

Bob stared at the train. “Please stay,” he said. “Not because we can’t manage without you. We can. Probably. But I’d rather not.”

The train’s first two carriages lit up.

Mallory rubbed her thumb over the crease in her ticket. “It was me who applied for the job overseas. My parents weren’t making me go. I let you think that because it was easier.”

Alice sat down on a platform bench.

“Do you want it?” she asked.

“Yes.”

Bob sat beside her. After a moment, Mallory joined them.

The last carriage filled with warm yellow light. Its doors opened.

“Are we supposed to get on?” Bob asked.

Alice checked her ticket. The words had disappeared. In their place was a single line:

**RETURN JOURNEY**

They rode home together. Bob asked about the city Mallory would live in. Alice wanted to know whether the job came with holidays. Mallory answered until the windows grew dark, then rested her head against Alice’s shoulder.

When they climbed out of the return bin, it was nearly closing time.

Mallory borrowed a travel guide. Alice helped her find it.

Bob checked out a cookbook, carefully inspected its pages, and took them both home for dinner.

Alice found the key inside a loaf of bread.

“This,” she told Bob, holding it above the crumbs, “is why I don’t trust artisan bakeries.”

Bob took off his glasses. The key was silver, no longer than his thumb, and warm from the oven. A paper tag tied to it read: **CLOCK TOWER. MIDNIGHT. COME HUNGRY.**

“Could be a promotion,” he said.

At five minutes to midnight, they found Mallory waiting beneath the clock tower with a picnic basket.

“You’re late,” she said.

“We’re early,” Bob replied.

“Not by that clock.”

Above them, the hands spun backward.

Alice held up the key. “You put this in my bread?”

“I needed someone curious enough to come and sensible enough to bring Bob.”

Mallory led them to a little door behind the tower. The key turned, and a staircase unfolded into the dark.

At the top stood a machine of brass wheels and trembling springs. One enormous gear was missing. In its place, wedged between two axles, was a burnt pie.

Bob stared. “That seems mechanically unsound.”

“My grandmother wound the town clock every Sunday,” Mallory said. “She also baked here. The machinery kept the pastry warm.”

“And you tried to continue the tradition,” Alice guessed.

“I confused two levers.”

Outside, a car rolled backward down the street. Rain climbed into the clouds.

Alice reached for the pie.

“Don’t,” Bob said. He studied the machine, then pointed to a narrow crank. “Hold that still.”

Alice gripped it with both hands. Mallory pulled out the pie. The machinery lurched, nearly lifting Alice off her feet.

“The missing gear!” Bob shouted. “Where is it?”

Mallory opened her picnic basket. Beneath a napkin lay a brass wheel, neatly dusted with flour.

“I thought it was a pastry cutter.”

Bob fitted it onto the axle. Alice let go.

The clock struck midnight.

Down in the street, the rain resumed falling. Somewhere, a driver leaned on his horn.

They sat on the stairs until their hands stopped shaking. Mallory passed around sandwiches.

Alice inspected hers carefully.

“There isn’t a key in it,” Mallory said.

“That’s what worries me. How do we get out?”

From far below came the small, definite click of the door locking.

Bob set down his sandwich.

“Next time,” he said, “we’re going to a normal bakery.”

Alice found the key inside a loaf of bread.

“That,” said Bob, the baker, “is not one of my ingredients.”

Across the counter, Mallory leaned forward. She was the town locksmith and had come to complain about a stubborn rye crust. The key was silver, warm, and shaped like a question mark.

“I know what it opens,” she said.

Bob sighed. “Of course you do.”

At midnight, the three of them met beneath the clock tower. Mallory led them around the back, where a narrow door stood between two bricks that had previously been touching.

“It appears once every thirteen years,” she explained.

“What’s inside?” Alice asked.

“Something lost.”

Bob checked his pockets.

“Not like that,” said Mallory.

Alice turned the key.

Beyond the door lay a room lined with shelves. On them rested a thousand small things: a blue mitten, a cracked teacup, a paper crown.

Bob stopped before a wooden spoon.

“My mother’s,” he whispered. “I thought we burned it with the old kitchen.”

He picked it up. Somewhere in the room, a woman laughed, and Bob pressed the spoon against his chest.

Mallory found a brass nameplate engraved with her father’s name. She rubbed her thumb over the letters.

Alice searched every shelf.

“What did you lose?” Bob asked.

“My courage.”

She said it lightly, but neither of them laughed.

At the far end of the room stood another door. Through its little window, Alice could see the harbor, a ship preparing to sail, and the faint pink edge of morning.

In her coat pocket was a letter offering her work across the sea. She had carried it for six months.

“I don’t think courage comes on a shelf,” Mallory said.

Alice looked back at the narrow entrance. Beyond it waited her familiar street, her familiar room, her familiar life.

“Will you write?” Bob asked.

Alice nodded.

Mallory pressed the silver key into her hand. “Then go before you talk yourself out of it.”

Alice opened the harbor door.

Behind her, Bob called, “And complain about the bread! Wherever you go, it won’t be as good as mine.”

She was still laughing when she stepped aboard.

Alice discovered the door on a Tuesday, behind a shelf of books nobody borrowed.

“Was that there yesterday?” she asked.

Bob, the town librarian, looked up from repairing an atlas. “Definitely not. Yesterday that was Geography.”

The door was narrow and green, with a brass sign:

**LOST THINGS. KNOCK ONCE.**

Alice knocked twice.

“Why?” Bob whispered.

“In case they lost the first knock.”

The door swung open.

Behind a desk sat Mallory, wearing a red coat and an expression of professional disappointment.

“Name?”

“Alice.”

Mallory searched a drawer. “You lost a blue mitten, six arguments, and the ability to whistle.”

“I never could whistle.”

“Exactly. Very thoroughly lost.”

Bob stepped forward. “I’m missing a cat.”

“Description?”

“Orange. Disagreeable. Answers to Professor, unless you need him.”

Mallory reached beneath the desk and produced an orange cat, who immediately bit Bob’s sleeve.

“Professor!” Bob said happily.

Alice peered past Mallory. Shelves stretched into darkness, crowded with umbrellas, keys, and glass jars full of shimmering light.

“What’s in those?”

“Lost afternoons. Forgotten dreams. Things people meant to say.”

“Are you in charge of all this?”

“For now.”

Something in Mallory’s voice made Alice look more closely. The red coat was too small at the wrists. Beneath the desk stood a battered suitcase.

“What have you lost?” Alice asked.

Mallory stopped sorting papers.

“Nothing.”

Professor jumped onto the desk and knocked over a ledger.

Under **MALLORY**, in faded ink, was a single entry:

**THE WAY HOME.**

“I came through when I was little,” Mallory said. “The clerk went to find it. He never returned. Someone had to stay.”

Bob closed the ledger gently. “Who says?”

Mallory pointed to a framed notice.

**SOMEONE MUST MIND THE LOST THINGS.**

Alice lifted it from its hook and turned it over. The back was blank. So was the wall behind it.

“I hang notices in the library,” Bob said. “Mostly so people will stop moving the chairs.”

For the first time, Mallory smiled.

She picked up her suitcase. At the threshold, she hesitated.

“What if my home isn’t there anymore?”

“Then we’ll start with dinner,” Alice said.

Mallory stepped through.

Behind them, the green door vanished. In its place stood a shelf of atlases.

Bob examined the shelf. Alice examined Mallory, who was staring at the late sunlight in the library windows.

“Well,” Bob said, “we should probably find you a map.”

But Mallory had already set down her suitcase.

“For dinner,” she asked, “do I need one?”

Alice found the key inside a loaf of bread.

She discovered it with her teeth, which put her in a poor mood before the adventure had properly begun.

“Someone’s trying to tell us something,” Bob said.

“Someone owes me a dentist,” Alice replied.

Across the bakery counter, Mallory stopped counting coins.

“What does the key look like?”

Alice held it up. It was brass, with a tiny moon cut into its head.

Mallory locked the shop door.

Bob glanced at Alice. “That seems promising.”

“That seems criminal,” Alice said.

“My grandmother baked that loaf,” Mallory explained. “She used to hide things when she was worried someone would steal them.”

“Used to?”

“She died yesterday.”

For a moment, the bakery was quiet.

Then Bob said, gently, “Did she leave you anything else?”

Mallory reached beneath the counter and produced a folded note.

*When the river knocks, let it in.*

That evening, the three of them went down to the old mill. Alice brought a lantern. Bob brought a rope. Mallory brought the note, though she had already memorized it.

The river was swollen with rain. Water struck the mill’s wooden sluice gate in three sharp beats.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

Beside the gate stood a small iron door. Its lock was shaped like a moon.

“I would like the record to show,” Alice said, “that I preferred the bakery.”

Mallory turned the key.

Behind the door was a wheel. Together, they forced it around. The sluice gate lifted, and river water rushed beneath the mill.

Something enormous began to turn.

Inside, gears groaned awake. A belt shuddered overhead. Then a row of dusty bulbs flickered on, illuminating shelves crowded with tins.

Bob opened one.

Seeds.

Every tin held seeds, labeled in Mallory’s grandmother’s careful handwriting: beans, squash, barley, apples. Varieties nobody in the valley had grown for years.

On a workbench lay another note.

*The bakery is yours. So is the garden, if you want it.*

Mallory sat on the dusty floor and cried.

Bob pretended to study the machinery. Alice sat beside her.

At last, Mallory wiped her face. “I don’t know how to grow any of this.”

“I do,” Bob said. “Some of it, anyway.”

Alice picked up a tin marked *winter wheat*.

“And I,” she said, “know what not to put in bread.”

By spring, they had planted the field behind the mill. Bob made the rows crooked, Alice complained about her knees, and Mallory kept forgetting which patch was which.

But things grew.

When the first wheat was ready, Mallory baked three small loaves. She set them on the counter while Alice and Bob watched.

“No surprises?” Alice asked.

“Just bread.”

Alice broke hers open to check. Then she passed half to Mallory, and they ate it while it was warm.

Alice found the key inside a loaf of bread.

“That’s a health violation,” Bob said.

“That’s an invitation,” Mallory said.

They stood in Alice’s kitchen, staring at the little brass thing among the crumbs. Tied to it was a paper tag:

**CLOCK TOWER. MIDNIGHT. BRING SOMETHING YOU REGRET.**

“It could be a prank,” Bob said.

But that night, he came anyway.

Alice brought an unopened letter from her sister. Bob carried the watch he had stolen from his father at seventeen. Mallory arrived empty-handed.

“Nothing?” Alice asked.

“Nothing portable.”

At midnight, the tower door opened before they touched the key.

Inside, a staircase spiraled upward into a room full of clocks. Behind them, the door clicked shut.

A voice emerged from the machinery.

“One regret may be undone. The price is the memory of everyone who shared it.”

Bob gripped his watch. Alice pressed the letter against her coat.

Mallory looked up.

“Last winter,” she said, “I told someone a secret that wasn’t mine.”

Alice went still.

Her sister’s last letter crackled beneath her hand.

“You?” she whispered.

Mallory nodded.

Bob stepped between them, then realized there was nowhere useful to stand.

“I thought she should know,” Mallory said. “Then I thought if I waited long enough, you’d both forgive each other.”

“You let me blame her.”

“Yes.”

The clocks stopped.

“Choose,” said the voice.

Alice imagined opening the letter without anger. Sunday dinners restored. Her sister laughing in the kitchen again.

Then she looked at Mallory, who was crying without trying to hide it.

“Would she remember confessing?” Alice asked.

“No.”

“Would I remember that she came here?”

“No.”

Alice took the brass key from her pocket and laid it on the floor.

“Then open the door.”

Outside, dawn was beginning to pale the rooftops.

Bob turned his father’s watch over in his hand. “I suppose I could just give this back.”

Alice opened the letter. Mallory waited at the edge of the square, far enough away to be dismissed.

When Alice finished reading, she folded the pages carefully.

“I’m going to my sister’s,” she said.

Mallory nodded and started to leave.

“Not with you,” Alice added. “Not today.”

Mallory stopped. “All right.”

Bob walked Alice to the station. By the time her train arrived, he had written three different messages to his father and sent the shortest one.

Mallory stayed behind to return the key to the bakery. She had a few questions for the baker.

This time, she intended to ask them aloud.

Alice found the key inside a loaf of bread.

“That,” said Bob, who had baked it, “is not one of my ingredients.”

Mallory leaned across the bakery counter. The key was black iron, its teeth shaped like tiny houses. A paper tag hung from its bow.

*For the door you’ve been avoiding.*

All three looked toward the blue door behind the flour sacks.

It had appeared on Tuesday. Alice had blamed Bob. Bob had blamed the landlord. Mallory, who delivered the mail, had quietly stopped bringing letters to the bakery.

“You know something,” Alice said.

“I know lots of things.”

“About the door.”

Mallory took off her cap. “That too.”

Years ago, the three of them had planned to leave town together. Alice would draw maps, Bob would cook aboard ships, and Mallory would write letters from places nobody back home could pronounce.

Then Alice’s father grew ill. Bob inherited the bakery. Mallory bought a sensible pair of boots.

They had never discussed the plan again.

Alice fitted the key into the lock.

Beyond the door lay a harbor at sunrise. Tall ships rocked against their ropes. Somewhere, someone was selling oranges in a language none of them knew.

Bob gripped the counter.

“How long has that been there?”

“Since Tuesday,” said Mallory.

“No. How long have you known?”

Mallory looked at her boots. “Since I found one in the post office.”

Alice turned. “You have a door too?”

“Green. Behind the lost parcels.”

Bob swallowed. “Mine’s in the pantry.”

For a moment, only the harbor spoke: gulls, bells, water against stone.

“I can’t leave forever,” Alice said.

“Neither can I,” said Bob.

Mallory studied the paper tag, then turned it over.

On the back, in very small handwriting, were three words:

*Then start smaller.*

Bob untied his apron.

Alice fetched her sketchbook.

Mallory put her cap back on and, for the first time in years, tipped it at a daring angle.

They hung a sign in the bakery window.

*Gone for a walk. Back tomorrow.*

Then they stepped through together.

Bob brought the bread.

Alice found the key inside a loaf of bread.

She discovered it just before breakfast, when her knife struck something that definitely wasn’t a walnut.

“Don’t touch it,” Bob said.

Alice held it up. “You might have said that before I touched it.”

Across the table, Mallory quietly put on her coat.

Alice noticed. Alice noticed most things.

“Sit down, Mallory.”

Mallory sat.

Outside, rain ticked against the bakery windows. Inside, the three friends stared at the little brass key.

Bob leaned closer. “That opens the clock tower.”

“The clock tower has been locked for thirty years,” Alice said.

“Thirty-one,” said Mallory.

Alice folded her arms.

Mallory sighed. “I stole it.”

“From whom?”

“The mayor.”

“Why?”

Mallory glanced at the wall clock. It read seven minutes past eight. It had read seven minutes past eight since Alice bought the bakery.

“Because he’s been stealing our time.”

Bob looked at his watch.

“Not that kind,” Mallory said. “The good bits. The moments you wish would last longer. He keeps them in the tower.”

Alice wanted to laugh. Instead, she remembered her father teaching her to knead dough: his hands over hers, the flour on his sleeves. She could remember the lesson, but not his voice.

She set down the key.

“Show us.”

***

The tower contained no gears.

Glass jars lined the walls from floor to ceiling. Inside each floated a small, flickering light.

Bob lifted one marked **BOB — FIRST SNOWFALL**.

Suddenly, he was laughing.

He clapped a hand over his mouth, astonished. “I remember. I thought the whole sky was falling down, and my mother said she’d catch it.”

Alice searched the shelves until she found her father’s name.

She opened the jar.

“Not too much flour, love,” his voice said. “Let it stick a little.”

Alice stood very still.

Mallory waited by the stairs, keeping watch.

“How do we put them back?” Bob asked.

Mallory took a hammer from her coat.

Alice wiped her eyes. “You planned this.”

“Most of it.”

“Why hide the key in my bread?”

“The mayor searched my house.”
